periods.activity_title: From Tallies to Ten Symbols — Our Number Story

tasks_in_class.description: Look at the picture. Estimate and write the number of each of the following objects: (a) Oranges (b) Bangles (c) Laddoos (d) Barfi (e) Bindis (f) Bananas.

time_bands.activity: The teacher narrates the story of how humans counted — cave tallies, groupings of 5, 10, 20, 60 — up to the ancient Indian invention of ten symbols (0–9). The role of zero as a place-holder is discussed with the class: 'What happens if we have no zero? How do we show an empty place?' Students share ideas aloud.

Let us Do Q1, p.16 ("Estimate and write the number of each object...."). Students study the illustrated bazaar scene and write their estimates for oranges, bangles, laddoos, barfi, bindis, and bananas. Partners compare their estimates and discuss whose is closer and why.

The class discusses strategies used — grouping by rows, clusters, or columns in the picture. The teacher draws out how grouping in tens (the same idea behind the decimal system) makes counting and estimating easier, linking back to the historical narrative.

periods.teacher_notes: Begin by showing a few tally marks on the board and asking students to count them, then ask how their ancestors might have counted without a number system. A common error is treating estimation as guessing randomly — nudge students to look for equal-sized groups in the picture before writing a number.

periods.activity_title: Climbing and Sliding — Numbers on the Board

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Play (fill missing numbers), p.17
tasks_in_class.description: Fill the missing numbers on the snakes and ladders board.
Which number will you reach if you take the ladder from 13?
You are standing on 96. Which number on the die will take you to the snake's mouth?
Show the number written on the tail of the longest snake using bundles and loose sticks.

time_bands.activity: The teacher displays or refers students to the partly completed snakes-and-ladders board. Let us Play (fill missing numbers), p.17 ("Fill the missing numbers on the snakes and ladders board."). Students work individually to fill in the gaps, skip-counting along each row.

Let us Play Q1, p.17 ("Which number will you reach if you take the ladder from 13?") and Let us Play Q3, p.17 ("You are standing on 96. Which number on the die will take you to the snake's mouth?"). Students reason about successor and predecessor positions, then share their thinking aloud — 'How did you figure out the die value?'

Let us Play Q4, p.17 ("Show the number written on the tail of the longest snake using bundles and loose sticks."). Students identify the tail number, gather matchsticks, and bundle them in tens to represent the number concretely. They record their bundle drawing in the notebook.

Additional practice from Let us Play Q2, p.17 may be assigned as classwork or teacher-directed oral work. The class discusses what patterns they notice when moving along rows: 'What changes and what stays the same as you count across a row?'

periods.teacher_notes: Additional practice: Let us Play Q2, p.17 ("If you are on the snake at number 25, which number will you reach?") — note this and Q3 are structurally similar; use either for paired discussion or additional classwork as the class needs. A common error is confusing the snake's head and tail — remind students the snake always takes you down from head to tail.
materials: Matchsticks or bundled sticks (tens and ones)

periods.activity_title: The Talking Pot and Ten Bundles of Ten

tasks_in_class.description: Complete the Talking Pot exchanges: I said 39, Pot said ___; I said ___, Pot said 90; I said 63, Pot said ___; I said ___, Pot said ___.
Fill in the blanks: use matchstick bundles (Making 100 table) and draw jumps on the number line to show 65+35=100 and make 100 by different jumps.
Use matchstick bundles and a ginladi to make 100 in different ways. Fill the table: 60 and 40 makes ___, 45 and ___ makes 100, ___ and 25 makes 100, ___ and 85 makes 100.

time_bands.activity: The teacher introduces the Talking Pot: it always says the next number. Let us Think (Talking Pot), p.18 ("Complete the Talking Pot exchanges: I said 39, Pot said ___...."). Students work in pairs — one says a number, the partner is the Pot. The class then fills in the four exchanges on the page.

Let us Do Q1, p.19 ("Fill in the blanks: use matchstick bundles and draw jumps on the number line to show 65+35=100...."). Students physically bundle ten sticks into a group of ten, and then group ten such bundles to see 100. They draw the complementary jumps on the number line strip.

Let us Do Q2, p.19 ("Use matchstick bundles and a ginladi to make 100 in different ways...."). Students use the ginladi (abacus-like tool) and bundles to show 60+40, 45+55, 75+25, 15+85 and complete the table. They share at least two different 'ways to make 100' with a partner.

A quick count round the class: the teacher calls a tens number, and students say its complement to 100 — '30!'... '70!'. This oral game consolidates the complementary-pairs idea from the bundles and number-line work.

periods.teacher_notes: Having grouped matchsticks in tens to count large collections, students are now ready to group ten bundles of ten to see 100 as a unit — make sure every student has handled the physical bundle before moving to the number line. A common error is writing the complement incorrectly when the ones digit is non-zero (e.g. writing 45+65 instead of 45+55); the number line jump helps students self-check.

periods.activity_title: Flower Petals, Seedfuls, and Matchbox Mysteries

tasks_in_class.description: Write numbers in the blank spaces inside the flower petals so that the numbers in each petal add up to 100.
Open a full box of matchsticks. Estimate the number, count them, check how close your estimate was, and find how many boxes get close to 100 matchsticks.
Take a handful of seeds (kidney beans, chickpeas). Estimate the number, count them, and find how many handfuls get close to 100 seeds.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q3, p.20 ("Write numbers in the blank spaces inside the flower petals so that the numbers in each petal add up to 100."). Students work on the flower petal puzzle individually, then compare solutions with a neighbour — multiple correct answers are possible and celebrated.

Let us Explore Q1, p.20 ("Open a full box of matchsticks. Estimate, count, check, and find how many boxes get close to 100...."). Groups open a matchbox, write their estimate, count the sticks carefully by organising into groups of ten, then compare estimate to count. They record the gap.

Let us Explore Q2, p.20 ("Take a handful of seeds. Estimate, count, and find how many handfuls get close to 100 seeds."). Each student takes a handful of seeds, estimates, then counts in tens. Groups pool handfuls to approach 100, recording their findings.

periods.teacher_notes: The flower petal task allows many correct answers — encourage students who finish quickly to find a second arrangement. A common error in the exploration tasks is random guessing before looking at the quantity; prompt the class to group objects in tens first and then revise their estimate before the final count.
materials: Seeds — kidney beans or chickpeas (per student / group)

section_titles: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O
periods.activity_title: One Bundle of a Hundred — Entering Three Digits

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do (fill table 101–110 + number line), p.21
tasks_in_class.description: Fill in the blank spaces in the table (100 and 1 makes ___… 100 and 10 makes 110 — number names and numerals) and fill the number line from 100 to 124.
Identify bundles and loose sticks in the H-T-O matchstick table and write the corresponding numbers. Extend the table in your notebook till 150.

time_bands.activity: The teacher places one hundred-bundle (ten bundles of ten) on the desk and names it the H (hundreds) position. Students observe the three-column matchstick table (100s | 10s | 1s) in the textbook. The teacher reads aloud the first row: 'One hundred-bundle, zero ten-bundles, one loose stick — one hundred and one, 101.'

Let us Do (fill table 101–110 + number line), p.21 ("Fill in the blank spaces in the table and fill the number line from 100 to 124."). Students complete the table rows for 101 through 110, writing both the number name and numeral. They then fill the number line from 100 to 124, marking each notch.

Let us Do Q1, p.22 ("Identify bundles and loose sticks in the H-T-O matchstick table and write the corresponding numbers. Extend the table to 150."). Students read each row of the bundle table and write the numeral. They extend the table independently in their notebooks, drawing H-T-O bundles for numbers up to 150.

periods.teacher_notes: The key conceptual move in this unit is recognising that 100 functions as a single new unit in the H column — just as ten ones became one ten-bundle, ten ten-bundles now become one hundred-bundle. A common error is writing the numeral without the hundreds digit (writing '13' for 113); reinforce H-T-O column reading every time a student reads a row.
materials: Matchstick hundred-bundle (ten bundles of ten, bound together)

section_titles: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O
periods.activity_title: Matching Bundles, Talking Pot, and the 100–150 Line

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do (match numbers to bundles), p.23
tasks_in_class.description: Match the numbers 101, 116, 110, 100, 140 with the correct bundles and loose sticks.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do (number line 100–150 + show numbers), p.23
tasks_in_class.description: Fill blank spaces on the number line (100–150). Show: place an arrow on 125, make a tree on 112, make a smiley on 149, put a cross on 137.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do (match numbers to bundles), p.23 ("Match the numbers 101, 116, 110, 100, 140 with the correct bundles and loose sticks."). Students examine five bundle pictures and draw lines to the matching numerals. They then explain one match aloud: 'I see one hundred-bundle, one ten-bundle, six loose sticks — that is 116.'

Let us Think (Talking Pot 127–150), p.23 ("Complete the Talking Pot table: 127→128, 109→___, 134→___, 105→___, ___→150, 100→___."). Students work in pairs — each takes one row and explains whether the hundreds or tens or ones digit changes. The class discusses the row where the tens digit must roll over (109→110).

Let us Do (number line 100–150 + show numbers), p.23 ("Fill blank spaces on the number line (100–150). Show: place an arrow on 125, make a tree on 112, a smiley on 149, a cross on 137."). Students fill the number line then mark all four symbols. Partners check each other's placements.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have worked with the H-T-O matchstick table are now connecting bundle pictures to numerals — ensure the matching task is read column by column (H first, then T, then O) rather than visually guessed. A common error in the Talking Pot for three-digit numbers is incrementing the tens instead of the ones (writing 137 for 127+1); ask 'which column changes when we add one?'

section_titles: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
periods.activity_title: Clap, Snap, Pat — Playing the Place-Value Body Game

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Play (Clap, Snap and Pat), p.24
tasks_in_class.description: Play in two teams: one team shows a three-digit number using clap (100), snap (10), and pat (1); the other team guesses the number.

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do (table 150–159, extend to 200), p.24
tasks_in_class.description: Fill the blank spaces in the counting table from 150 to 159 (pictorial form, matchstick bundles, number sentence, number name). Extend to 200 in your notebook.

time_bands.activity: Let us Play (Clap, Snap and Pat), p.24 ("Play in two teams: one team shows a three-digit number using clap (100), snap (10), and pat (1); the other team guesses the number."). Team A performs a sequence of claps, snaps, and pats for a chosen number in the 150–200 range; Team B writes the number on their slate. Roles swap. The teacher signals each round and ensures students connect the body action to the H-T-O column.

Let us Do (table 150–159, extend to 200), p.24 ("Fill the blank spaces in the counting table from 150 to 159...."). Students complete the provided table rows (pictorial bundle drawing, number sentence, number name, numeral) for 150–159, then extend the same four-column pattern in their notebooks toward 200.

A quick oral count: the teacher calls out a number between 150 and 200 and individual students name the number that is one more. This consolidates the sequential counting pattern built in the table and body-rhythm game.

periods.teacher_notes: The body-rhythm game encodes place value as physical memory — one clap always means one hundred, regardless of where the game starts. A common error is treating each clap as a count of ten; reinforce that one clap = one hundred-bundle, and have a student show one hundred-bundle on the desk to anchor the action.
materials: Slates or mini whiteboards (for Team B guesses)

section_titles: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
periods.activity_title: Jumping by Fives and Twenties on the Number Line

tasks_in_class.description: Draw jumps of 5 on the number line (100–150) and write the numbers in the given spaces.
Continue the jumps of 20 and write the missing numbers on the number line (100–200).
Fill in the 1-less/number/1-more table for 160, 129, 187, 134, 158.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q1, p.26 ("Draw jumps of 5 on the number line (100–150) and write the numbers in the given spaces."). Students open to the number line, identify the starting point and jump size, arc each jump of 5, and label. They count aloud as they arc: '100, 105, 110…' The teacher asks: 'How many jumps did it take to reach 150?'

Let us Do Q2, p.26 ("Continue the jumps of 20 and write the missing numbers on the number line (100–200)."). Students extend the jump-of-20 pattern already started on the longer number line, filling in each labelled notch. They compare the two number lines: 'What is different about jumping by 5 and jumping by 20?'

Let us Do Q3, p.26 ("Fill in the 1-less/number/1-more table for 160, 129, 187, 134, 158."). Students complete each row, paying careful attention to numbers where the ones digit is 0 (1-less changes the tens) or 9 (1-more changes the tens). Partners swap and check.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have counted in tens and skip-counted to 100 are now extending those skip patterns into the 100–200 range — the jumping number line makes the additive pattern visible as equal arcs. A common error on Q3 is writing 1-less of 160 as 169 or 150; reinforce that 'one less' moves only one step back on the number line.

section_titles: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
periods.activity_title: Many Ways to Make a Number — Bundles, Ginladi, Line

tasks_in_class.description: Show at least two different ways of making the following numbers: (a) use matchstick bundles to make 125; (b) make 145 using a ginladi; (c) make 170 on a number line.
Fill the empty boxes in the multi-representation table (number, pictorial form, matchstick bundles, number sentence) for 114, 132, a pictorial form, 172, 108, 30 more than 150, and 160.

time_bands.activity: Let us Do Q4, p.27 ("Show at least two different ways of making the following numbers: 125 with bundles, 145 on a ginladi, 170 on a number line."). Students work at their desks with matchstick bundles and the ginladi, constructing each number in at least two ways. They record a quick sketch of each representation beside the task.

Let us Do Q5, p.27 ("Fill the empty boxes in the multi-representation table for 114, 132, a pictorial form, 172, 108, 30 more than 150, and 160."). Students move across each row — numeral, picture, bundle, number sentence — filling whichever cells are blank. The teacher circulates and asks: 'How did you know what goes in the number sentence column?'

An unhurried pair-share: each student shows a partner one row from the table and explains how the four representations connect. The teacher takes two or three examples and records them briefly on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: The goal of this unit is flexible multi-representation — students should feel that the same number can live in bundles, on a ginladi bead-frame, and as a jump on a number line simultaneously. A common error is filling the number sentence column as H+T+O added as single digits (1+2+5 instead of 100+20+5); reinforce place value of each digit during the pair-share.

section_titles: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
periods.activity_title: Placing Numbers — Marking the Full 100–200 Line

homework.book_ref: Let us Do at Home (stones), p.25
homework.description: Write the numbers in order on the stones (150…158…163…167…177…182…189…199).

time_bands.activity: The teacher draws a blank number line from 100 to 200 on the board and asks: 'Where would 150 sit? Where would 175 sit?' Students estimate positions and explain their reasoning. This oral warm-up builds the spatial sense needed for the main task.

Let us Do Q6, p.28 ("Mark the following numbers on the number lines: (a) 109, 112, 124, 134, 146; (b) 155, 163, 178, 189, 198; (c) 125, 142, 153, 174, 199."). Students work through all three number lines, locating each number by estimating its position between the nearest labelled landmarks and marking it with a dot and numeral. Partners compare placements and discuss any differences.

The teacher selects two or three numbers from different number lines and asks: 'Is this number closer to 100 or 150? Closer to 150 or 200?' This benchmarking discussion connects the number-line work to estimation reasoning. The homework task — ordering numbers on stones — is introduced and read together.

periods.teacher_notes: Students who have placed numbers on shorter number lines (100–124, 100–150) are now working across the full 100–200 range — encourage them to first mark the midpoint 150 as a reference before locating other numbers. A common error is spacing numbers evenly without regard for their actual distance from landmarks; ask 'Is 109 near the beginning or the end of this line?'

section_titles: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation

tasks_in_class.book_ref: Let us Do at Home, p.25
tasks_in_class.description: Fill a small container with seeds. Estimate how many seeds are in it, count them, then guess how many container-fills get close to 200 seeds.

time_bands.activity: Students examine a small container and a supply of seeds. The teacher asks: 'Without counting, how many seeds do you think fit in this container? How did you decide?' Students write their first estimate on a slip of paper. The class shares a range of estimates.

Let us Do at Home, p.25 ("Fill a small container with seeds. Estimate how many seeds are in it, count them, then guess how many container-fills get close to 200 seeds."). Students fill the container, count the seeds by grouping in tens, and record both the estimate and the actual count. They calculate or reason about how many fills would approach 200.

Groups share their counts and their 'number of fills' reasoning. The teacher records the different container counts on the board and asks: 'If your container holds 40 seeds, how many fills to reach 200? If it holds 25 seeds, how many?' The class discusses, connecting this to skip-counting by the container's count.

An unhurried close: each student writes one sentence — 'My container held ___ seeds. I need ___ fills to get close to 200.' This written record consolidates the estimate-count-scale chain from the concrete exploration.

periods.teacher_notes: This exploration task brings the chapter's number range to life through physical measurement and scaling — connecting the abstract 'double century' target to something the student has held in their hands. A common error is treating the scaling question as multiplication before students are ready; guide them toward repeated addition or repeated counting by the container's size instead.
materials: Seeds — kidney beans or chickpeas (large supply)

items.section_title: Building 100 — What is 100?
items.prompt: Draw matchstick bundles to show 65 and 35 on the grid on p.19. Then write the number sentence that shows they make 100 together.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Student draws 6 ten-bundles and 5 loose sticks for 65, and 3 ten-bundles and 5 loose sticks for 35; writes 65 + 35 = 100.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Group the tens first: 6 tens + 3 tens = 9 tens, then 5 ones + 5 ones = 10 ones = 1 ten, giving 10 tens = 100.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically bundle sticks before drawing; stretch: ask them to show one more pair that makes 100.

exercise.description: Fill in the blanks: use matchstick bundles (Making 100 table) and draw jumps on the number line to show 65+35=100 and make 100 by different jumps.

items.section_title: Building 100 — What is 100?
items.prompt: Riya opens a matchbox and counts 46 sticks. About how many such matchboxes would she need to get close to 100 sticks?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 2 matchboxes (46 + 46 = 92, which is close to 100; 3 boxes would be 138, much further away).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Double the count and compare to 100: 46 × 2 = 92, which is the nearest to 100.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student thinks one box already holds 100 sticks, confusing the box count with the target.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has not thought about the size of the box count and guessed a middling number.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student confused the place-value idea of 'ten' with the number of boxes needed.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student act it out by adding 46 twice on a number line; stretch: ask what would happen if the box held 30 sticks instead.

exercise.description: Open a full box of matchsticks. Estimate the number, count them, check how close your estimate was, and find how many boxes get close to 100 matchsticks.

items.section_title: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O
items.prompt:
Look at the H-T-O table below. Write the number that matches each row.

Row 1: 1 hundred-bundle, 2 ten-bundles, 3 loose sticks
Row 2: 1 hundred-bundle, 0 ten-bundles, 7 loose sticks
Row 3: 1 hundred-bundle, 4 ten-bundles, 0 loose sticks

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read H digit first, then T, then O: H hundreds + T tens + O ones gives the three-digit numeral.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student build each row with physical bundles before writing the numeral; stretch: ask them to add one more row of their own choice.

exercise.description: Identify bundles and loose sticks in the H-T-O matchstick table and write the corresponding numbers. Extend the table in your notebook till 150.

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt: Show the number 165 in TWO different ways. You may draw matchstick bundles, show it on a number line, or write a number sentence. Label each way clearly.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Any two correct representations — for example: (1) 1 hundred-bundle, 6 ten-bundles, 5 loose sticks drawn in H-T-O columns; (2) a number line with an arrow at 165 between 160 and 170; or a number sentence 100 + 60 + 5 = 165.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose 165 into 1 hundred, 6 tens, 5 ones and represent each part using the chosen tool.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use physical bundles or ginladi first, then sketch what they made; stretch: ask them to show a third way and explain which they find easiest.

exercise.description: Show at least two different ways of making the following numbers: (a) use matchstick bundles to make 125; (b) make 145 using a ginladi; (c) make 170 on a number line.

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt: Meena fills a small cup with seeds and counts 25 seeds in it. She wants to collect close to 200 seeds. About how many cupfuls does she need? Show your thinking.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 8 cupfuls (8 × 25 = 200 exactly), so 8 cups gets her to exactly 200 — accept 7 or 8 with reasoning.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count on repeatedly by 25 from 0 until reaching or passing 200: 25, 50, 75, 100, 125, 150, 175, 200 — eight counts.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw a number line and mark hops of 25 starting from 0; stretch: ask what would happen if the cup held 30 seeds instead.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do at Home, p.25
exercise.description: Fill a small container with seeds. Estimate how many seeds are in it, count them, then guess how many container-fills get close to 200 seeds.

items.section_title: The Story of Our Numbers
items.prompt: In the ancient Indian number system, which symbol made it possible to write a number like 100 using only two different symbols (1 and 0)?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Zero, the place-holder — it signals an empty position so the digit 1 can mean one hundred.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Without zero in the tens and ones places, the numeral 100 cannot be written; zero marks the empty positions.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student recalls the grouping-by-5 tally system but has not connected zero to the decimal place-value idea.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is thinking of the earliest counting method described in the story, not the innovation of the decimal system.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses having a symbol for ten (like Roman numerals) with having a place-holder that makes ten redundant.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to write '100' and say what the two zeros are doing; stretch: ask them to explain why zero was considered a revolutionary invention.

exercise.description: Look at the picture. Estimate and write the number of each of the following objects: (a) Oranges (b) Bangles (c) Laddoos (d) Barfi (e) Bindis (f) Bananas.

items.section_title: Snakes and Ladders — Numbers to 100
items.prompt: On a snakes and ladders board, Anu is standing on 93. The snake's mouth is at 98. Which number must Anu roll on the die to land exactly on the snake's mouth?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the difference between the snake's mouth and the current position: 98 − 93 = 5.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student subtracted the tens digit instead of computing the distance: 9 − 3 = 3 rather than 98 − 93.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student may have counted on from 94 instead of 93, missing the starting square.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student over-counted by one, perhaps counting the starting square as one step.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count forward on a number line from 93 to 98 using finger-hops; stretch: ask what the die would need to show if Anu were on 91 instead.

exercise.description: You are standing on 96. Which number on the die will take you to the snake's mouth?

items.section_title: Building 100 — What is 100?
items.prompt:
The Talking Pot always says the number that comes just after the number you say. Complete the table.

I said → Pot said
47 → ___
___ → 70
89 → ___
___ → 100

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 1: Pot said 48; Row 2: I said 69; Row 3: Pot said 90; Row 4: I said 99.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 1 to 'I said' to get Pot's answer; subtract 1 from Pot's answer to find what was said.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count forward one step on a number line; stretch: ask them to make two more rows of their own for the Talking Pot.

exercise.description: Complete the Talking Pot exchanges: I said 39, Pot said ___; I said ___, Pot said 90; I said 63, Pot said ___; I said ___, Pot said ___.

items.section_title: Building 100 — What is 100?
items.prompt: A flower petal has two numbers: 38 and ___. The two numbers must add up to 100. What is the missing number?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the complement: ones 8 + 2 = 10 (write 2, carry 1), tens 3 + 6 + 1 = 10, giving 100.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student added 38 + 52 = 90, not 100 — they forgot to include the tens carry.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student rounded 38 to 30 and subtracted from 100 to get 70, then subtracted 2 getting 72 — a place-value error.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student may have computed 100 − 38 with a ones-digit error, writing 68 instead of 62.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw the number-line jump from 38 to 100; stretch: ask them to find two more petal pairs that add to 100.

exercise.description: Write numbers in the blank spaces inside the flower petals so that the numbers in each petal add up to 100.

items.section_title: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O
items.prompt: Which of the following shows 1 hundred-bundle, 1 ten-bundle, and 6 loose sticks?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 116 — one hundred-bundle gives the digit 1 in the hundreds place, one ten-bundle gives 1 in the tens place, and six loose sticks give 6 in the ones place.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read H-T-O columns in order: 1 hundred, 1 ten, 6 ones → 116.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student read 1 hundred and 6 in the ones but placed the ten-bundle in the ones column, giving 160 instead of 116.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student swapped tens and ones, reading 6 tens and 1 one instead of 1 ten and 6 ones.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student ignored the ten-bundle and read only the hundred and the ones, giving 106.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student build the number with physical bundles and then read H-T-O aloud before writing; stretch: ask them to describe what 116 + 1 would look like in the H-T-O table.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do (match numbers to bundles), p.23
exercise.description: Match the numbers 101, 116, 110, 100, 140 with the correct bundles and loose sticks.

items.section_title: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O
items.prompt:
The Talking Pot says the number that comes just after. Complete the table for three-digit numbers.

I said → Pot said
139 → ___
___ → 120
109 → ___

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 1 to the ones digit; when the ones reach 10, carry 1 to the tens — the tens digit increases by 1.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use a number line marked 100–150 to count one step forward or back; stretch: ask what the Talking Pot would say if someone said 149.

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt: In the Clap-Snap-Pat game, a student does 1 clap (= 100), 7 snaps (= 10 each), and 3 pats (= 1 each). What number did they show?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Multiply each action count by its place value and add: 1×100 + 7×10 + 3×1 = 173.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student concatenated the counts as digits (1, 7, 3) without applying place values, giving 1073.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student added 100 + 70 = 170 and dropped the 3 pats (ones).
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student reversed the tens and ones counts, treating 3 as tens and 7 as ones.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student physically act out the claps and snaps and pats, then tally each column; stretch: ask them to design a Clap-Snap-Pat sequence for 185.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Play (Clap, Snap and Pat), p.24
exercise.description: Play in two teams: one team shows a three-digit number using clap (100), snap (10), and pat (1); the other team guesses the number.

items.section_title: Snakes and Ladders — Numbers to 100
items.prompt:
Which number is missing from the sequence on a snakes and ladders board row?

51, 52, ___, 54, 55

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 53 — the numbers count upward one at a time; the number between 52 and 54 is 53.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Count forward by 1 from 52 to find the missing number: 52 + 1 = 53.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student continued past 55 instead of filling the gap, showing a direction error.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student looked at the tens digit and subtracted, not recognising the sequential pattern.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student moved backward by ten instead of forward by one, confusing row and column movement on the board.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count aloud on fingers from 51; stretch: ask them to write the next five numbers after 55.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Play (fill missing numbers), p.17
exercise.description: Fill the missing numbers on the snakes and ladders board.

items.section_title: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O
items.prompt: What number does '100 and 8 makes ___' complete to?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 108 — 100 and 8 more gives 108, written as 1 in the hundreds place, 0 in the tens, 8 in the ones.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Place 1 in H, 0 in T, 8 in O to read the numeral as 108.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student ignored the hundred and read only the 8, writing 18 — the hundreds digit is lost.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student wrote the hundred and the 8 as two separate numbers joined, giving 1008 — not understanding place value.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student placed 8 in the tens column instead of the ones column, giving 180.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student write H, T, O across the top and fill in each digit one at a time; stretch: ask what 100 and 12 makes.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do (fill table 101–110 + number line), p.21
exercise.description: Fill in the blank spaces in the table (100 and 1 makes ___… 100 and 10 makes 110 — number names and numerals) and fill the number line from 100 to 124.

items.section_title: Numbers from 100 to 150 — Place Value H-T-O
items.prompt:
Mark each number on the number line below with the symbol shown.
• Arrow (↑) at 118
• Star (★) at 103
• Cross (✕) at 145

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Arrow between 110 and 120, closer to 120 (at 118); star just after 100 (at 103); cross near 150 (at 145).
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Find the nearest labelled landmark on each side and estimate the position proportionally between them.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first locate the nearest ten below each number before marking; stretch: ask them to write one more number between 140 and 150 and mark it.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do (number line 100–150 + show numbers), p.23
exercise.description: Fill blank spaces on the number line (100–150). Show: place an arrow on 125, make a tree on 112, make a smiley on 149, put a cross on 137.

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt: In a counting table from 150 to 159, what is the number name for 156?

teacher_guide.method_one_line: Read the hundreds digit first (one hundred), then the remaining two digits as a two-digit number (fifty-six).

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student swapped the tens and ones digits, reading 56 as 65.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added 10 to the correct answer, reading 166 instead of 156.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student dropped the hundreds component entirely and read only the last two digits.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student cover the leading 1 and read the last two digits first, then put 'one hundred and' in front; stretch: ask them to write the number name for 163.

exercise.book_ref: Let us Do (table 150–159, extend to 200), p.24
exercise.description: Fill the blank spaces in the counting table from 150 to 159 (pictorial form, matchstick bundles, number sentence, number name). Extend to 200 in your notebook.

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt: On a number line from 100 to 200, a frog jumps by 20 each time starting from 100. What number does the frog land on after 4 jumps?

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student draw four arcs of 20 on a blank number line starting from 100; stretch: ask how many jumps of 20 it takes to reach exactly 200.

exercise.description: Continue the jumps of 20 and write the missing numbers on the number line (100–200).

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt: What is 1 more than 179?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 180 — the ones digit goes from 9 to 0 and the tens digit increases by 1: 179 + 1 = 180.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Add 1 to the ones: 9 + 1 = 10, write 0 in ones and carry 1 to tens: 7 + 1 = 8, giving 180.

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student subtracted 9 from 179 instead of adding 1.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added 10 instead of 1, giving 189.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student subtracted 1 instead of adding 1.

teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student count one step forward on the number line from 179; stretch: ask what 1 more than 199 is and explain what happens to all three digits.

exercise.description: Fill in the 1-less/number/1-more table for 160, 129, 187, 134, 158.

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt:
Fill in the table. The first row is done for you.

Number | Number sentence | Number name
114 | 100 + 10 + 4 = 114 | One hundred and fourteen
___ | 100 + 30 + 2 = ___ | ___
172 | ___ | ___
items.visual_stimulus:
| Number | Number sentence | Number name |
| 114 | 100 + 10 + 4 = 114 | One hundred and fourteen |
| ... | 100 + 30 + 2 = ... | ... |
| 172 | ... | ... |

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Row 2: Number 132, number sentence 100 + 30 + 2 = 132, name One hundred and thirty-two. Row 3: Number 172, number sentence 100 + 70 + 2 = 172, name One hundred and seventy-two.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Decompose each digit by its place value (hundreds, tens, ones) and read the name by saying the hundred, then the remaining two digits.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: let the student use the H-T-O column template to fill each digit before writing the sentence; stretch: ask them to add a fourth row of their own choice.

exercise.description: Fill the empty boxes in the multi-representation table (number, pictorial form, matchstick bundles, number sentence) for 114, 132, a pictorial form, 172, 108, 30 more than 150, and 160.

items.section_title: Numbers from 150 to 200 — Counting, Jumping, Multi-Representation
items.prompt: Mark the numbers 162, 178, and 195 on the number line below. Write each number above its mark.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: 162 sits between 160 and 170, slightly left of centre; 178 sits between 170 and 180, near the right; 195 sits between 190 and 200, near the right.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Locate the nearest labelled ten below each number, then estimate how many ones to count forward from that landmark.
teacher_guide.inclusivity: Support: ask the student to first circle the nearest labelled number below each target before marking; stretch: ask which two of the three numbers are closest together and how they know.
